Designed to Shine: The Italian Prosecco That Doubles as a Statement Piece

Whether you’re planning a milestone celebration or simply gathering a small group of friends for an impromptu dinner party, the details can feel overwhelming. There’s a menu to set, a table to shape, a guest list to curate, and, of course, drinks to pour.

Choosing a bottle that looks like it belongs at the table adds to that convivial feeling, which is why Brilla!, premium Italian Prosecco is the preferred choice for so many hosts.

Combining authentic Italian craftsmanship with modern style, Brilla! Prosecco DOC Rosé and Prosecco DOC are an effortless choice to pair alongside classic entertaining fare, from freshly shucked oysters to shrimp cocktail to charcuterie. 

With a delicate and complex bouquet of pear, green apple, and lemon as well as floral notes of acacia and rose, the Rosé is fresh and light on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

Made from Prosecco’s iconic white grape, Glera, known for producing light-bodied, high-acid wines with neutral to fruit-forward aromatics, along with Pinot Noir, the blend offers a round and full-bodied structure. This makes it perfect to enjoy as an aperitif, but also positions it as an ideal accompaniment to Prosciutto e Melone (Cured Ham & Cantaloupe) and grilled fish entrées.

Meanwhile, the crisp and dry profile of the Prosecco DOC feels fresh on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

The pronounced peach and green apple notes set the tone for a decadent evening of al fresco summer dinners and pair impeccably with seasonal favorites likegrilled chicken and peaches. And the iconic sound of popping open a bottle only prolongs guests’ desire to linger at the table for hours, talking long after the meal is complete. 

Don’t be surprised if Brilla!’s distinctive, jewel-inspired bottle design comes up as a topic. The conversation-starting, covetable object reflects the meaning of the Italian word (“to shine”). It’s the ideal choice for hosts who understand that the eyes eat first, and that the style of a tablescape influences how guests feel about the menu, the company, and the celebration to come. 

“Brilla was designed to stand apart long before the first pour,” says a representative from the brand. “Its distinctive patented textured bottle, inspired by the brilliance of cut crystal, transforms every bottle into a statement piece—reflecting the sparkle, elegance, and celebration found inside.”

The Brilla! bottle is the result of a design study that goes beyond a simple wine bottle. Its patented texture is reminiscent of a diamond, and echoes a classic gemstone drop shape.

In the world of diamonds, drop-shaped stones are among the most distinctive and difficult to craft; the symmetry, which is achieved with hard work and dedication during processing, is key to the overall beauty of this stone.

Worn as a ring, earring, or pendant, the shape provides a characteristic elegance with which no other diamond cut can compete; it enhances, romantically and gently, the wearer’s form.

This makes each bottle an effortless gift, requiring no additional gift wrap or presentation.

As a natural bridge between the worlds of fashion, design, and hospitality, Brilla! is a beloved choice for making celebratory, Prosecco-based cocktails, which can signal the start of a brunch or aperitif hour in style.

Some of the most common and popular examples include the Aperol Spritz, Bellini, Mimosa, and Negroni Sbagliato, with Prosecco.

In each of these cocktails, Brilla! adds a layer of sophistication and complexity, and sets the tone for an elevated, elegant occasion that guests will associate with a design-minded host.

title: Was the Wine Industry Worrying About the Wrong Generation?
summary:
New data debunks the myth that Gen Z is drinking less. Baby boomers, on the other hand, are a different story.

The post Was the Wine Industry Worrying About the Wrong Generation? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Gen Z alcohol consumption has climbed to 74%, debunking early fears that younger adults are abstaining entirely.
  • Conversely, Baby Boomers show the steepest drop in alcohol consumption, becoming the true generation of moderation.
  • Younger consumers prioritize social experiences and higher quality drinks over traditional wine cellaring or heavy drinking.

The wine industry can breathe easy. According to a newly-released report from beverage analytics firm IWSR, the alcohol consumption rate amongst Gen Z has risen to 74%, up from 66% three years ago. 

After all the hand-wringing about whether this generation, which includes people born between 1996 and 2010, would ever come around to drinking, the stats are showing that they are. More than 84% of Gen Z (of legal drinking age) have consumed cocktails in the last six months, which is more than any other generation. Gen Z has the second-highest beverage alcohol participation rate (77%) of any generation, slightly behind Millennials. 

“The industry spent a long time asking whether younger consumers were interested in wine, when the more interesting question was why it didn’t seem like they were,” says Tynan Pierce, the wine director at Yes Society, the wine club founded by Antica Terra’s Maggie Harrison. “I don’t think younger drinkers were rejecting wine. I think they were rejecting the way wine was being presented to them.”

Baby boomers, however, are a different story. According to the report, boomers (ages 62 to 80) registered significant declines across all consumption metrics. That demographic—long a stronghold for wine sales—has the lowest consumption rate of any generation. 

While the industry has been fretting about Gen Z sales, a key generation was aging out of wine. Have wine pros been worrying about the wrong generation?

The Kids Are Alright

The good news is that 20-somethings are spending money in the alcohol sector. Sure, wine is splitting sales with ready-to-drink cocktails, coolers, and the like, but they’re not vaping instead or abstaining entirely, as early reports suggested.

“The narrative that Gen Z is the generation of moderation is now conclusively debunked,” says IWSR President and Managing Director Marten Lodewijks.

However, as the IWSR report points out, this young generation is interacting with alcohol differently than their elders did.

For one, Gen Z is a cocktail crowd—84% have consumed cocktails in the last six months. They center alcohol around occasions: 18% reported that their last drink was enjoyed in the context of gatherings with five or more people (so, parties.)

Drew Brady, wine director at Ravi DeRossi’s Long Count (and one of Wine Enthusiast’s 2023 Future 40), has noticed that what Gen Z lacks in drinking culture knowledge, they make up for with a love of events, nights out, and occasions. “It feels like drinking is less of an automatic part of the week—the way it was for us—and more attached to a chosen night out,” Brady says. “

While they may not be collecting as much, or spending in the same way, Gen Z is proving to be particularly appreciative of some of wine’s best qualities—storytelling and connection. 

“They want to know who made the wine, how it was made, and why it works on the menu,” he says. “How does this contribute to their experience? A bottle does not need to be famous, but it does need to feel alive, distinctive, and worth remembering.”

“The biggest shift we’re seeing is from accumulation to curation,” says Tyson. “Previous generations often viewed wine through the lens of building a cellar, while younger consumers tend to view wine as something to be opened, shared, and experienced.”

A recent study funded by Bacardi seconded this, finding that Gen Z tends to drink earlier in the day rather than late at night, at occasions rooted around socializing. The Bacardi report also found that 70% of emotionally engaged consumers will spend twice as much on brands they connect with.

“Gen Z is not necessarily rejecting alcohol,” says Charles Ewudo, founder and CEO of PCN Entertainment, a nightlife giant spanning clubs, cocktail bars, and drinks brands. “They are rejecting outdated ways of discovering and engaging with brands … The alcohol industry has viewed Gen Z’s changing relationship with drinking as a challenge, but I think it’s important to recognize that Gen Z is also showing brands where the future of consumer behavior is headed.”

The IWSR’s Lodewijks confirms this: “While Gen Z consumers are creating new patterns for engaging with beverage alcohol, the evidence demonstrates that Gen Z consumers enjoy drinking at roughly the same levels as the rest of society.”

OK, Boomer

While the kids are alright, the IWSR’s report flagged that boomers are not. Drinking continues to decline among the demographic. Boomers reported the smallest number of drinking occasions of any generational cohort and reported consuming the smallest number of drinks when they do drink (an average of 2.6 drinks per occasion). 

“Boomer drinking has been tailing off for several years,” says Lodewijks. This is unsurprising for consumers hitting their 60s and 70s—people grow older, health goals shift.

“These latest Bevtrac results, however, show bigger-than-expected drops in boomer drinking across all major metrics,” he continues. “If this trend continues, it may actually be the boomers, not Gen Z, who deserve the title ‘generation of moderation.”

Moderation Moment

Adding to the fuddle of this all, a global moderation movement has impacted how all demographic groups interact with alcohol. 

49% of Gen Z drinkers reported they are likely to listen to government health guidelines. While consumption rates are steady across all generations, frequency of occasion and amount consumed on each occasion are down—3.9 drinks per occasion, down from 4.4 drinks in 2025.

Thankfully, this reflects a general shift towards a less-but-better approach to alcohol consumption. Last year’s IWSR BevTrac report noted that Gen Z consumers buy less, but do spend more when they make a purchase.

“Gen Z is not consuming mass quantities at the low end, and instead drinking higher quality wines,” says Tim Willard, partner at wine bar Madeira Park. “This generation seems undaunted by the mystery of wine—their comfort zone is exponentially larger than previous generations.”

He finds his restaurant is a playground for all generations, so he gets a front-row seat to the way people actually engage with wine. 

“I think the most important shift is Gen Z’s attitude on quality with little regard for the appellation system,” he says. “It’s actually having a bottom-up effect on older generations, who seem more open to trying wine from less familiar-to-them grapes and places.”

The Takeaway

Is the fact that boomers are spending less on wine a reason to panic? Not likely. This generational shift reflects a changing of a guard, a signal of where big wine powers should shift focus towards. 

“Boomers have historically been some of the most loyal alcohol consumers, but loyalty does not mean immunity to shifting behaviors,” says Ewudo. “As this generation gets older, health, wellness, lifestyle changes, and moderation are impacting consumption habits.”

In short? “The industry cannot assume that yesterday’s loyal customer will consume the same way tomorrow. “

title: At Some Bars, 23 Is the New 21
summary:
To keep rowdy teenagers and inexperienced palates away, a growing slew of cocktail bars across the world are upping the age requirement to 23.

The post At Some Bars, 23 Is the New 21 appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • In Puerto Rico, some cocktail bars are enforcing restrictions above the legal drinking age of 18 to discourage rowdy behavior.
  • Higher age requirements are gaining traction worldwide at bars in cities like Dublin, Stockholm, and New York.
  • Bar owners use these policies to curate a more mature atmosphere for older patrons who appreciate craft cocktails and tip.

Tucked away in the cobblestoned streets of Old San Juan, Puerto Rico, La Factoría— named the best bar in the Caribbean by North America’s 50 Best Bars—is a complex of seven interconnected spaces, a veritable nightlife multiverse that includes a quiet wine bar, a salsa club with live music, and a candle-lit speakeasy. Though every space has its own appeal, for many people, the bar’s biggest draw is what it doesn’t have: guests under 23 years of age.

Puerto Rico‘s legal drinking age is 18, so weekends in nightlife districts typically see crowds of teenagers and young adults bar hopping or drinking in the street. Some are locals and some are wide-eyed American mainlanders who’ve come to the island to get their first (legal) drink. Increasingly, some high-end Puerto Rican bars are now choosing to close their doors to these youngsters, instead searching for customers who might be more interested in enjoying thoughtfully crafted cocktails than in getting drunk. 

High age restrictions are slowly gaining popularity around the world. Dublin, Ireland, boasts the 23-plus Vintage Cocktail Club, and Stockholm, Sweden, has the 24-plus Soap Bar. On New York’s Upper East Side, The Auction House has barred entrance to anyone under 25 on Fridays and Saturdays since 1993. Earlier this year, Dirty Franks, a Philadelphia dive bar, imposed a 25-and-over rule after a surge in fake IDs, including one for Ben Franklin.

These policies are still far from the norm. But, given La Factoría’s astonishing success despite (or perhaps because of) its restriction, other Puerto Rican bars may follow suit. “We made that decision from the very beginning and maybe it’s spreading,” says Leslie Cofresí, La Factoría’s co-owner. “Maybe it’s all our fault.”

A Bar Scene Grows Up

Fifteen years ago, Puerto Rican cocktail culture was just beginning to come into its own. “It’s a new thing here, having so many cocktail bars,” says Mike Norat, a local World Class-awarded bartender and industry veteran. Instead, most people bought beer at casual open-air spots called chinchorros and drank it in public squares. And rather than specialty cocktails, bars offered simple mixed drinks like rum and coke or vodka with orange juice.

In 2013, La Factoría opened its doors, turning the Puerto Rican bar scene on its head. While there were already great cocktail bars—like the Santurce neighborhood’s legendary Santaella—La Factoría showcased its intentionality right off the bat as the first bar to deny entry to groups of people who could legally drink. “[The age policy] was a way to attract the type of customer that we wanted, and to create a more curated experience,” states Cofresí. And however frustrated this made the youths of Puerto Rico, objections to the policies don’t generally have legal standing, as age isn’t usually a protected class outside of the workplace.  

To Norat, this approach makes total sense. “[Teenagers] didn’t know how to drink, they got too drunk, they looked for trouble, they didn’t spend a lot of money.” Of course, this behavior also deters many older customers, for whom being surrounded by drunk teens is the very definition of hell.

At Aurora, a newly-opened cocktail bar with its own 23-plus age restriction, the thinking is similar. “[Younger people] are starting to drink, starting to go out, exploring and getting to know their palate,” says Ivanna Ortiz, Aurora’s operational manager. “And the cocktail world is so complex and vast that experience has taught us that, at that age, they don’t have the mentality necessary to enjoy a cocktail, or to appreciate the process.” 

Meanwhile, bar staff also benefit from these raised age restrictions. Ortiz claims that it’s common for these young drinkers to complain about unfamiliar tastes and prices, or to mock elaborate garnishes and modern techniques like carbonization or clarification. And because they don’t understand what goes into these higher drink prices, they often don’t leave tips.

Other bars and clubs around the island—including the famous Fifty Eight in Condado’s La Concha Resort—have a minimum age of 21. Some, like Club Brava, switch to 21 on weekends, like many 18+ clubs do in the U.S. to avoid underage drinking. While every 18-year-old in Puerto Rico can legally drink, this helps keep rowdy teenagers away. 

While Aurora initially considered going for the more common 21-plus restriction, Ortiz says the owner ultimately decided on 23 to “play it safe.”

Is the Policy Worth the Trouble?

Of course, not everyone is happy about the restrictions. Cofresí recalls instances in which people have gotten angry or left scathing reviews after being turned away at the door. He still defends the decision: “The people that come in are expecting the restriction. It’s sort of a guarantee of the experience.”

Aurora has had a similar response. “We’ve had negative reactions from people who don’t understand why they can’t come in even if they’re legal adults,” Ortiz acknowledges, but adds, “Our loyal customer base mostly loves that we have those filters because they feel more comfortable.”

title: Albariño Is Taking Over the World. These Top-Rated Bottles Span the Globe.
summary:
While staying true to the flavors of its Iberian roots, crisp, clean Albariño has found a home across the globe.

The post Albariño Is Taking Over the World. These Top-Rated Bottles Span the Globe. appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
If refreshing, high-acid whites are generally what you reach for (looking at you, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling lovers), then Albariño is right up your alley. Native to the Iberian Peninsula, this zesty and crisp wine pairs beautifully with a variety of dishes, yet remains light enough to enjoy without a full meal on deck.

Albariño: From the Iberian Peninsula to the Rest of the World

Albariño is a white grape variety native to and most commonly grown in northwest Spain (Galicia specifically), as well as the northwestern Portuguese regions of Monção and Melgaço, where it goes by the name Alvarinho.

As producers around the world look for grape varietals that can adapt to warmer climates, many see Albariño as a saving grace. Characterized by high levels of natural acidity and thick skins, which allow it to grow well in humid, maritime-influenced regions, it’s frequently vinified as a monovarietal wine, though sometimes is blended with the Loureiro grape in less expensive styles.

Albariño wine is typically dry, with a lean structure and aromas of citrus (specifically lemon, lime, and grapefruit), honeysuckle, orange zest, yellow apple, and mango, plus a bit of saline-driven minerality. Styles may vary from producer to producer—some may err on the citrusy and herbaceous side, whereas others may lean more floral and tropical.

“The thing that makes Albariño really fun to drink is that there is a nice juxtaposition of the floral and tropical aromatics versus the tart, racy acidity on the palate,” says Chris Gaither, Master Sommelier and service director at San Francisco’s Ungrafted SF.

Pairing Albariño with Food

The wine’s high levels of acidity and fruit-forward nature make it an excellent pairing with a variety of fresh foods, from herbaceous green salads to salty fish-based dishes, seafood towers, and more. Tinned fish, oysters, simply-prepared shellfish, milder white fish, Galician octopus (or “pulpo a la gallega”), and similar offerings all pair well.

In addition to seafood, look to Vietnamese and Thai dishes, as well as a variety of soft cheeses, to highlight the Albariño’s acidity and texture.

Max Working, senior portfolio manager for Spain, Portugal, and Greece for Skurnik Wines, explains that Albariño is best enjoyed chilled—but not too cold—and generally either as an apéritif or (ideally) with something from the sea.

Travis Padilla, the New York City-based sommelier, agrees. He believes it’s best enjoyed chilled, with good company, on a hot day. “It has the ability to transport you to the Spanish coastline with its briny, citrus qualities—a literal vacation in a glass,” he says.

Gaither is a bit more specific in his temperature preferences, serving Albariño somewhere around the 46-degree Fahrenheit mark. This allows the wine’s freshness and citrus flavors to shine. “Pop open a bottle at a table full of food and friends to get them hooked, and also get the party going,” he says. “And don’t forget to invite me!”

We’ve rounded up a few of our top-rated Albariño bottles from around the world below. So uncork a bottle, pour a glass, and enjoy.

Spain

Albariño grows around the world today, but scientists believe the grape originated in the Rías Baixas region of Spain’s Atlantic coast. Expressions from this area are all-time favorites for Tonya Pitts, a sommelier and Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large. 

“Its fog, rolling hills, and landscape are reminiscent of Ireland with its seaside influence along the Atlantic Ocean,” Pitts says. “The soil is decomposed granite, so the vineyards have excellent drainage, and the vines are happy. There is an incredible amount of rainfall, and it snows in the winter. Doesn’t that sound like a groovy, mystical place to grow grapes?”

Albariño grown in this region is “high-energy and vibrant with aromas of Mexican lime, Meyer lemon, green guava, and notes of green apple, dried herbs, sedimentary rock, and saline on the nose,” Pitts says. “The flavors on the palate repeat the nose with a mouth-watering mixture of youthful fruit, high acid, and mineral goodness. Super refreshing.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Rodrigo Mendez & Alberto Orte 2023 Muti Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Candied aromas of caramel apple and butterscotch open on the nose along with tropical notes of mango tea and pastry cream. More reserved on the palate than the nose, the wine reveals tangy acidity that leans into crushed stone and freshly-shaved lemon peel. Pair with turkey burgers and falafel. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Reggie Solomon

$44 The Cellar D’Or

Forjas del Salnés 2024 Leirana Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Pastry dough, tangerine peel and chamomile aromas waft from the glass along with a touch of yogurt and meadow grass. Citrus and subtle hints of sea salt breaststroke across the midpalate which finishes in a pool of river stone and lemon peel. Pair with oysters, moules frites and Croque Monsieur. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — R.S.

$34 JJ Buckley

Torres 2024 Pazo das Bruxas Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Vibrant notes of underripe green and yellow fruit open into an energetic, mineral-driven palate. The oceanic influence comes through clearly, underscored by the wine’s bright acidity. This is a lovely showing for the level. 92 Points — Brandon Borcoman

$27 Wine.com

Bodegas La Caña 2023 La Caña Navia Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

A full, robust nose accented by oceanic nuances carries onto a palate that remains somewhat tightly wound. The wine is certainly pleasurable now, though it feels destined to show at its best a few years down the road. Remember folks: don’t be afraid to age your Albariño! 93 Points — B.B.

$35 Wine Chateau

Portugal

In Portugal, Albariño is called Alvarinho. It’s used to make Vinho Verde, “a fantastic dry white unique to the country. Crisp but with a creamy texture, topped by a mineral touch from the granite soil of this Northern region,” according to Roger Voss, a Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large who reviews wines from the region.

For years, Vinho Verde has been a go-to for affordable crisp white wines. Recently, however, the overall quality has risen dramatically, Voss reports, driven by top producers such as Anselmo Mendes. “The best Alvarinho comes from the Minho Valley on north-facing vineyards,” Voss notes. Look for bottles labeled with the sub-regions of Monção and Melgaço.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Soalheiro 2024 Primeiras Vinhas Alvarinho (Vinho Verde Monção e Melgaço)

This wine, with its tropical fruit aroma, is rich and finely textured. It has a hazelnut and citrus flavor that gives the wine both freshness and ripeness. Drink the wine from 2026. Suitable for vegans. Editors’ Choice. 92 Points — Roger Voss

$28 Wine.com

Anselmo Mendes 2024 Muros Antigos Alvarinho (Vinho Verde Monção e Melgaço)

The wine’s ripe citrus fruits are full and bursting with vitality. The intensity is enhanced by orange zest flavors. The wine has a kiwi and white peach aroma that emphasizes its ripeness. Drink from 2026. 91 Points — R.V.

$17 PJ Wine

West Coast

New World Albariño producers are giving Old World stalwarts a run for their money. This is especially true of vintners along the West Coast of the United States.

“Though a relatively recent arrival, Albariño shows tremendous promise across many corners of the West Coast, as the grape retains a freshness and green-fruit snap even when grown in warmer zones,” says Matt Kettmann, a Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large. He notes that it “really excels” in exciting ways throughout the cooler pockets of the Central Coast, from Monterey down to Santa Barbara. 

“The most notable region would be the San Luis Obispo coast, where the Edna Valley’s  mountains-meet-sea geography bears a striking resemblance to Rías Baixas,” Kettmann says. “Some say that this is historic Albariño’s New World counterpart, and the vivid wines that emerge from this maritime climate are indeed reminiscent of Spain’s best.” 

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Cadre 2024 Sea Queen Albariño (San Luis Obispo Coast)

This might be the best vintage yet for this exciting white wine brand, which is showcasing SLO Coast’s potential like few others. Aromas of honeydew, kiwi, grass and rainy cement make for a detailed nose. The fun but serious palate sizzles with acidity and clings with texture, showing green apple, pomelo and margarita flavors. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Matt Kettmann

$28 Wine.com

Morgan 2024 Albariño (Arroyo Seco)

This is a fantastic bottling, starting with a baking soda-like minerality on the nose that evolves into lemon and lime blossom aromas. The acidity is vibrant on the palate, staying almost prickly while cutting into the fresh lime, guava and cut grass flavors. 94 Points — M.K.

$30 Morgan Winery

Matilija Wines 2023 Albariño (Santa Barbara County)

Sharp lines of lime meet with flashes of riper nectarine on the nose of this bottling. The palate is extremely textural, as grippy edges frame the bright citrus and brisk stonefruit flavors. 93 Points — M.K.

$37 The Good Land Wine Shop

South America

Not surprisingly, Albariño excels in South American wine-growing regions that are similar in character to Rías Baixas. Uruguay, in particular.

“Surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, Uruguay enjoys a climate with moderate temperatures year-round and abundant rainfall,” says Jesica Vargas, a Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large who reviews wines from South America. “Albariño, which arrived in Uruguay in the early 2000s, has thrived in this vibrant South American country.” 

Vargas notes that most of the wines are crisp, floral, and fruit-forward with a light saline accent. However, winemakers are still in the process of experimenting with different styles and planting in new regions. “I’m excited about the future of Albariño in Uruguay,” she says.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Bodega Garzón 2025 Reserva Albariño (Maldonado)

This Albariño offers a youthful character, with a nose of orange zest and a crisp palate. Subtle hints of grapefruit and saline notes create a tasty mix of flavors that linger in the medium finish. 90 Points — Jesica Vargas

$20 Wine.com

title: 10 Years of Frosé: The Slush Rush That Changed Summer Forever
summary:
We chatted with the inventors of frosé about that fateful New York summer—and what the cocktail’s enduring success says about the drinks landscape.

The post 10 Years of Frosé: The Slush Rush That Changed Summer Forever appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Few years in recent memory are as heavily romanticized as 2016. Hamilton had just debuted on Broadway, Instagram was still a space where filtered images felt fun instead of dystopian, Beyoncé dropped Lemonade, and both politics and the planet were less noticeably on fire. It was also the year frosé entered our collective lexicon.

In the age of martinis trying to masquerade as caprese salad and water getting the protein treatment, the original recipe for frosé is still one of the most compelling arguments for doing less.

Remembering Frosé Frenzy

Combining just three ingredients—rosé wine, rosé vermouth, and puréed strawberries, dispensed from a slushie machine—the frozen concoction resonated with drinkers all over the country, almost instantly.

“Rosé was everywhere that summer,” recalls Justin Sievers, the godfather of frosé and former general manager at Bar Primi’s original Bowery location in New York City. Now co-owner of Café Mulberry, Sievers says he came up with the recipe in 2016 after spending time tinkering with the frozen drink machine that Bar Primi had just purchased for frozen Negronis.

“Rosé was the wine of the season, and New York was in the middle of a brutally hot stretch,” he says, “so I started wondering if there was a way to turn rosé into a slushie to make it even more refreshing.”

Since that 2016 summer of frosé, as the hospitality industry has been rocked by generational behavior shifts, tariff rollercoasters, and the after-effects of Covid, brands and bartenders increasingly feel the pressure to prioritize virality over the drinker experience. The more gimmicky a cocktail launch, the more likely someone will buy it, try it, and make a video reviewing it. There’s a widespread sense that a straightforward drink doesn’t hold the same intrigue (or content potential).

Coincidentally, it was frosé’s simplicity that led to its virality. The content flourished.

“The name was memorable, the color practically demanded to be photographed, and most importantly, it was genuinely delicious and refreshing. Almost overnight, we had a line down the block,” Sievers recalls. “This was before ‘line culture’ was even a thing in New York City, and I was frantically trying to source more machines just to keep up with the demand.”

Josh Nadel, beverage director of NoHo Hospitality, which owns Bar Primi, believes that the genesis of frosé includes “a strong helping of curiosity augmented with a bit of mischief, alongside equal parts luck and intention.” Nadel says he watched Siever land on a blush-pink, slushie-type drink that still tasted like rosé. After realizing that the name “frosé” felt natural, it was clear that a star was born. 

During those first two summers, the Bar Primi team sold almost 940 frosés in a single weekend. “People were coming in, ordering a round, taking pictures, and leaving before they even finished their drinks,” says Nadel. “With machines running at both bars and in our prep kitchen, we barely kept up.” 

Over the years, demand has remained consistent, but at a more reasonable pace. “We are always surprised that winter sales, albeit not at summer levels, remain strong,” he adds.

The Drink That Lifted Multiple Tides

As publications from all over the world started catching wind of what Bar Primi was doing— Insider released a video about it that went viral, racking up around 10 million views in just a few days—Sievers says it hit him that frosé wasn’t just a fad or a micro-trend. It was breathing life into a classic cocktail category that had previously been relegated to boardwalks and casinos. And most importantly, it was easy to replicate at bars and restaurants everywhere, even without a seasoned bartender or beverage director on staff.

“It woke the sleeping frozen drink giant in contexts and locations which previously eschewed or excluded the category,” says Nadel. “Today, you are just as likely to find a frozen Negroni at a ’50 Best’ bar as you are a frozen margarita at a seaside taco bar. I’d say rather than inspiring a specific cocktail, it’s more the elevation and acceptance of the category as a whole.”

One of the most obvious side effects of frosé’s influence is the nationwide rise of the frozen spritz. Aperol’s big American marketing campaign during the summer of 2018 pushed the spritz as a go-to happy hour and patio hangout order. With so many bars and restaurants running slushie machines around the clock, the marriage of frosé and spritz was inevitable. 

The combination remains popular today. Houston’s Montrose Cheese & Wine makes a cult-favorite drink known as the Swurl, a 50/50 blend of frosé and sangria; Il Bruto, in Austin, serves a frozen Aperol spritz called the Fraperol Spritz. In Nashville, at the newly opened Capricious, located inside the Fairline Hotel, the cheerful frozen Campari and strawberry spritz has quickly become a summer favorite.

Just like studio executives struggle to resist a sequel to a best-seller, frosé’s success has been something of a siren call for bartenders and restaurant owners.

While it’s fairly easy to tell when a martini has been tinkered with, frosé’s slushie, rosy appearance makes it somewhat trickier to spot riffs on the original recipe. At Gurney’s Beach Club in Montauk, frosé is made with Aperol, vodka, orange bitters, lemon juice, and rose syrup. According to food and beverage director of operations Antonello Paganuzzi, as of this summer, it has become the second-best-selling drink on the menu, served in a generous 14-ounce cup.  

A few summers after frosé’s debut, Bar Primi started playing with frozen Lambrusco, blood orange, and melon; now, at Cafe Mulberry, Sievers layers the original recipe with a frozen matcha latte—he calls the resulting drink a Fratcha.

While these playful riffs on adult beverages have become summer standards, they were somewhat groundbreaking back in the simpler days of 2016. As the cost of living has skyrocketed, wars rage around the world, and once-in-a-lifetime climate events turn into annual occurrences, it’s no wonder a cocktail that appeals to all of our inner child continues to endure. It allows us to experience the child-like joy of downing an ice cream cone, sans spoon, with a little alcohol. Plus, if one drink could take you back to the way things were ten years ago, wouldn’t you order it?

title: Sonoma Wines Have Never Been This Excellent. Here’s What to Drink Right Now
summary:
While Sonoma may be among California’s most prolific wine regions, what really stands out is its range. These top-rated bottles prove it.

The post Sonoma Wines Have Never Been This Excellent. Here’s What to Drink Right Now appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Sonoma County is large. Very large. The region encompasses over a million total acres, stretching from the Pacific Ocean inland to the Mayacamas Range. It houses some sixty thousand acres of vines and over four hundred wineries. While Sonoma may be among the Golden State’s most prolific wine regions, what really stands out is its range. 

Chardonnay and Pinot Noir can be rich and opulent, complex and high-toned, and everything in between. Bordeaux varieties can be examples of pure power or charming nuance. Rhône varieties? Cal-Itals? German and Austrian varieties? You name it, someone in Sonoma has it planted. 

While Sonoma may be best known for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, it pays to get off the beaten path and try something new. Recent vintages in this diverse area have produced a tremendous crop of exceptional wines. It’s well worth taking a moment to examine what’s new in the region.

Weather Report

It’s hard to make blanket statements about the weather in a region as varied as Sonoma. Hot inland weather might be contrasted by fog in hillier, more coastal zones. Windswept ridges closer to the Pacific shield valleys and trap warm air. The Petaluma Gap opens to the ocean, allowing huge swaths of Sonoma Valley to “breathe.” 

Further complicating the climate is the fact that weather has become increasingly unpredictable. In 2022, a hot summer and oppressive heat dome around Labor Day forced many growers to make snap decisions around harvest time. The best of these wines are opulent but refined, embracing the decadence of the vintage. 

By way of contrast, 2023 was cooler and wetter than usual. Producers who favor long hangtime and gradual flavor development loved seeing later harvest dates. These wines bring a backbone of notable acidity and the best versions display extreme complexity. The recently released 2024s that are just hitting the market show a more “in-between” profile. Not too hot, not too cold, not too wet. Great examples show nuance and ripeness in tandem… a bit of a Goldilocks situation from a climate perspective.

Trend Report

One primary trend informs much of the innovation happening among Sonoma County’s winemakers in recent years: the gradual sway away from overly oaked and potently alcoholic styles. Instead of harvesting exclusively by sugar levels, producers in Sonoma are looking at acids, phenolic ripeness, and other markers to determine pick dates. The resulting wines possess greater balance, acidity, and freshness. 

Everywhere you look, you find improved farming methods. Sustainable, organic, regenerative, dry farming, and biodynamic vineyard practices are all part of the conversation. Low and no-till rows are becoming far more common, and permanent cover crops are increasing soil and vine health. When winemakers pair these more holistic vineyard practices with experimental varieties, plus the increased use of concrete, amphora, and larger format vessels, you see the picture of a region that embraces its history as a California standard bearer, but one that lets the site control the narrative.  

What to Drink Right Now

Here are some recently reviewed Sonoma wines to suit everyone’s taste, from your steak-loving uncle to the too-cool-for-school twenty-something in your life.

Aromatic Whites

Morning fog and cool nighttime temperatures help keep acids high in Sonoma County. That’s perfect for crisp, refreshing whites. Sauvignon Blanc certainly thrives here in an array of styles, but examples of White Pinot Noir, Vermentino, and many more are also worth seeking out.

Shared Notes 2024 Les leçons des maîtres Sauvignon Blanc (Russian River Valley)

This plush and seductive Sauvignon Blanc shows vibrant aromas of tart pineapple, apricot, ginger, lime, and orange blossom on the nose, while the opulent palate delivers flavors of ripe Meyer lemon, lime, lemongrass and pineapple sage through a long finish. There’s enough structure and tension here for a few years in the cellar. Cellar Selection. 94 points — Tom R. Capo

$95 JJ Buckley

Emeritus Vineyards 2024 Hallberg Blanc Pinot Noir (Russian River Valley)

The nose of this dry farmed White Pinot Noir brings aromas of Golden Delicious apple, candied ginger, lemon blossoms, and pineapple sage. The palate vibrates with energy and juicy acidity, singing with flavors of roasted pineapple, tart nectarine, and Ranier cherry that sit in a framework of pithy texture and bright florals through the finish. Editors’ Choice. 94 points — TRC

$45 Emeritus Vineyards

Reeve 2023 Vermentino (Sonoma Coast)

A big, beautiful nose of white flowers, lime peel and river rocks bursts from the glass of this Vermentino. The palate is focused and nervy, with loads of citrus, finishing with a wave of salty Meyer lemon that’s just like summer in a glass. 93 Points — TRC

$31 Wine.com

Chardonnay

From the Russian River Valley to the Petaluma Gap and up the hillsides of the Mayacamas, Sonoma is Chardonnay country. Some of California’s most famous examples come from these areas. Chardonnay is a chameleon, showing dazzling acidity in some expressions and rich structure in others. Sonoma County is capable of producing almost any version you can imagine.

Knights Bridge 2023 Kelley Chardonnay (Knights Valley)

A whisper of flinty reduction mingles with aromas of tangerine, caramelized pineapple, and white flowers on the nose of this Chardonnay. The palate is energetically acidic, with flavors of green apple, juicy lemon, and ginger, with pithy citrusy acid driving the finish. Editors’ Choice. 95 points — TRC

$110 Knights Bridge

Sangiacomo Wines 2023 Four Siblings Chardonnay (Sonoma Coast)

This sumptuous native yeast and concrete fermented Chardonnay delivers an explosive nose of nectarine, pineapple and white flower aromas. The palate delivers flavors of concentrated apple and stony minerality with biscuity notes from sur lie aging, energetic acidity and salty, pithy Meyer lemon lingering on the finish. 97 points — TRC

$70 Sangiacomo Wines

Croix 2023 Richard Dinner Chardonnay (Sonoma Mountain)

Absolutely gorgeous aromas of ripe Gala apple, ginger, crème brulee and pineapple sage swirl on the nose of this generous native fermented Chardonnay. The palate delivers plush, almost sensual texture, vibrant acidity and concentrated flavors of nectarine, cinnamon and caramel that intensify and soften in waves along the finish. Cellar Selection. 97 points — TRC

Pinot Noir

The Russian River Valley is one of the world’s best-known regions for Pinot, but areas like Petaluma Gap and West Sonoma Coast are carving out a reputation for consistently exceptional quality. Perhaps most interestingly, growers working in cooler zones within the Russian River Valley are crafting more aromatically intense and high-toned examples.

Blue Farm 2022 Gap’s Crown Vineyard Pinot Noir (Petaluma Gap)

Baked cherry, spiced berry coulis and cocoa powder aromas jump from the glass on the nose of this complex and rich Pinot. The palate brings concentrated cherry, cinnamon and fried shiitake flavors in a framework of soft tannin and raspberry lemon acidity. Best from 2028-2040. Cellar Selection. 95 points — TRC

Inquire with winery

Williams Selyem 2023 Terra de Promissio Vineyard Pinot Noir (Sonoma Coast)

Aromas of baked cherry, cranberry, nori, cedar and roses waft from the glass on the nose of this Pinot. The palate gives more concentrated berry character, with loads of floral energy and rich tannin that will soften with a little time in the cellar. Best from 2030-2045. Cellar Selection. 96 points — TRC

$110 Total Wine

Senses 2023 Bodega Thieriot Vineyard Pinot Noir (West Sonoma Coast)

This earthy and savory native fermented Pinot displays aromas of tart cranberry, nori, shiitake and plum skin on the nose, giving way to flavors of tart cherry, fried mushrooms, sandalwood and sage on the palate, with fresh orange peel acidity and echoes of clove along the finish. Best from 2030-2040. Cellar Selection. 97 points — TRC

Inquire with winery

Kanzler Vineyards 2023 One Fifteen Pinot Noir (Russian River Valley)

The nose of this Pinot leads with aromas of crushed black cherries, dark cocoa powder, violets and black tea, giving way to flavors of tart raspberry, cinnamon, nori and fried shiitake on the palate, with bouncy acidity and just a bit of grippy tannin at the end. Editors’ Choice. 95 points — TRC

Cabernet Sauvignon

Once thought of as Napa’s little cousin, Sonoma Cabernet Sauvignon is becoming a major player globally, with top examples rivaling the great wines of the world. Moon Mountain, Rockpile, and other high-elevation destinations are creating wines of substance, nuance, and character.

Far Mountain 2022 Montecillo Cabernet Sauvignon (Moon Mountain District Sonoma County)

Aromas of black plum, licorice, cracked pepper and flowers drive the nose of this Cabernet from a historic high elevation vineyard. The palate is layered with flavors of dusty cherry, cocoa powder, spiced plum compote, fresh flowers, and graphite that linger on and on and on. This needs time to unfold properly, best from 2030 on. Cellar Selection. 96 points — TRC

$100 K&L Wines

The Setting Wines 2022 Rockpile Ridge Vineyard Cabernet (Rockpile)

Bright, focused aromas of concentrated raspberry, mint and iron-laden earth erupt from the glass on the nose of this powerful Cabernet. The palate is sumptuous, giving velvety tannins, bright acidity and flavors of berry coulis, black plum, herb-spice mélange and violets that linger along the finish. Delicious now, this will reward patience. Best from 2030-2045. Cellar Selection. 98 points — TRC

Inquire with winery

Judge Palmer 2022 Monte Rosso Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon (Moon Mountain District Sonoma County)

The nose of this complex and enticing Cabernet gives aromas of dusty cherry, spiced plum compote, pencil shavings, cocoa, and flowers. The palate brings potent tannins balanced with mouthwatering acidity and flavors of blackberry gastrique, currants, cinnamon, and chopped mint leaves along with a compelling minute-long finish. Give this time to unfold in the cellar and it will become a showstopper. Cellar Selection. 95 points — TRC

$95 Emmitt-Scorsone

Something New

In a region with so much diversity of soil and climate, there’s a hillside for almost any variety. Thoughtful experiments like this amphora-aged Viognier, Carbonic Grenache, and seldom-planted Austrian red are well worth seeking out.

Jacuzzi 2024 Clarum White Blend (Petaluma Gap)

This amber-tinged, amphorae aged blend erupts from the glass with aromas of concentrated peach, lemongrass, Meyer lemon, and white flowers. The palate is decadent, with rich extraction, plush acidity, and flavors of green apple, lemon peel, jasmine, and tangerine thrumming through the finish. Editors’ Choice. 94 points — TRC

$45 Jacuzzi Wines

Smith Story 2024 BRAVE Grenache (Dry Creek Valley)

This carbonic Grenache is positively joyful, with bright strawberry, rose petal, and raspberry aromas exploding from the glass on the nose. The palate vibrates with crunchy tannins, juicy acidity and loads of berry and floral character. Perfect with a little chill and some chill tunes. 94 points — TRC

$40 Smith Story Wines

Ottavino 2023 Ricci Vineyard St. Laurent (Los Carneros)

Aromas of concentrated black cherry, bacon, violets and pencil lead drive the nose of this native fermented St. Laurent. The palate brings nervy acidity and balanced tannins, with flavors of sour cherry, fresh flowers and herbs mingling before a plushly textured finish. 93 points. 93 points — TRC

title: Vinho Verde Is the Crisp Summer Wine You’ve Been Looking For
summary:
No, Vinho Verde isn't actually green. Here's everything you need to know about the Portuguese region producing top-rated bottles.

The post Vinho Verde Is the Crisp Summer Wine You’ve Been Looking For appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
If there’s one thing to know about Vinho Verde—which in Portuguese translates to “green wine”—it’s that this wine isn’t green. While it’s a common misconception, Vinho Verdo simply refers to bottlings from a region in Portugal of the same name. (That name likely originated because wines from this area were historically released young.)

With tart acidity and a subtle fizz, these wines are perfect for sipping in the summer sun. Indeed, after getting to know them, you might make Vinho Verde your go-to wine region for warm weather. Here’s everything you need to know before picking up your first bottle.

What Is Vinho Verde?

Vinho Verde is a wine region wedged into the northwest corner of Portugal, just below the border with Spain. Similar to many other areas like Bordeaux or Rioja, these wines are often sold under the region name. In addition to its devilish green shadow, another common misconception about Vinho Verde is that the region only produces white wines, but the range of wines is actually just as wide as any other region.

“You can make white, red, rosé, vinegar, brandy, or sparkling wine as long as it’s made with autochthonous varieties,” says Tiago Soares, winemaker at Sapateiro winery in Vinho Verde. “If they are grown inside the region and have a spectrum of flavors that are expected for these wines, that’s Vinho Verde.”

But it hasn’t always been this way. Up until the ‘80s, most of the wines produced here were red because of local preference. However, he explains, once Portugal began exporting more wines, they discovered that the region’s style of light, acidic wine is better served by white varietals, and whites became more prominent.

“Most people associate Vinho Verde with a style of white wine which may be described as light, fresh, aromatic, and slightly [effervescent],” explains João Miguel Maia, producer of Portugal-based Casa de Vilacetinho winery. But these tasting notes can vary depending on the sub-region and the winemaker. Citrus, ranging from lime to lemon zest to grapefruit, is common, but some styles are more ripe with stonefruit and tropical flavors.

Regardless of color or flavors, all Vinho Verde wines have high acidity and relatively low alcohol. However, “the biggest differentiating feature of Vinho Verde wines is that they are lightly sparkling,” says Miguel Maia. “In the past, this fizziness was obtained through a natural second fermentation in the bottle, similar to a pét-nat.” Nowadays, winemakers often add carbon dioxide at the bottling stage to achieve the spritz-like texture.

So, Where Did the Name ‘Vinho Verde’ Come From?

“Some people think that the grapes are harvested early, or harvested when they’re green and therefore they make a green wine,” says Soares. “But it’s not necessarily because of that.” Nor is it because the region is verdant all year round, he adds.

The name likely comes from the fact that the wines were traditionally released young—within three to six months after harvest, Soares says. This lent them a fresh and light characteristic with high acidity and low alcohol. These days, Vinho Verde wines are still released at a young age, so the fresh qualities remain prominent today.

How and When to Drink Vinho Verde

“Vinho Verde are wines that should be consumed immediately due to their light flavor profile and delicate effervescence,” Anna-Christina Cabrales, Wine Enthusiast’s tasting director, says. “You don’t want the bottles to be too old, as they may fall flat or not feel as energetic.” 

With their light and fresh profile, Vinho Verde wines lend themselves particularly well to summertime settings and summery foods. Soares suggests pairing with spicy foods, as the wine’s fresh fizz acts as the perfect palate cleanser. Miguel Maia enjoys Vinho Verde alongside summery seafoods and salads, but he notes that they are equally delicious all on their own. Regardless of the time, place, or pairing, make sure to serve these wines with a good chill.

When it comes to Vinho Verde, your best bet is to hit your local bottle shop to pick up the freshest release. Nevertheless, we’ve pulled together some of our recent favorites to give you an idea of what to look for. Next time you’re in the market for a bright and zesty wine, keep these top-rated Vinho Verdes in mind. 

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Soalheiro 2024 Primeiras Vinhas Alvarinho (Vinho Verde Monção e Melgaço)

This wine, with its tropical fruit aroma, is rich and finely textured. It has a hazelnut and citrus flavor that gives the wine both freshness and ripeness. Drink the wine from 2026. Suitable for vegans. Editors’ Choice. 92 Points — Roger Voss

$28 Wine.com

Aveleda 2024 Solos de Xisto Alvarinho (Vinho Verde)

There’s a distinct gracefulness to this bottling, as genteel mixed citrus, apples, and melon rind lay a foundation for white flowers, white pepper, and wet rock on the nose. The underlying mineral note anchors the wine and lends a little gravitas. Calls out for sushi and will be excellent over the next 2-3 years. Best Buy. 91 Points — John Sumners

$23 Wine.com

Quinta da Pedra 2022 Graça da Pedra Alvarinho (Vinho Verde)

After a few years, Alvarinho deepens and matures well. That’s the case with this wine. It has a ripe lemon aroma that leads to a wine with richness and a touch of aging. It is ready to drink. Best Buy. 91 Points — R.V.

$17 MacArthur Beverages

Quinta de Santa Teresa 2022 Singular Portuguese White (Vinho Verde)

The Malvasia in the blend gives this wine a perfumed character. It lends the wine a nutty character balancing the wine’s soft acidity. Drink this attractive wine now. Organic. Editors’ Choice. 90 Points — R.V.

$12 Portugal Vineyards

Constantino Ramos 2024 Juca Loureiro (Vinho Verde)

There’s a bright intensity to this wine on the palate, as a beam of tart citrus and mineral undertones are filled out by aromatics of nectarine, coriander seed, and river stone. This will be just the thing for oysters and clams on the half shell or simply prepared sushi/crudo/ceviche. Ready to drink over the next 2-3 years. 90 Points — J.S.

$26 Divine Vintage

Casa de Vilacetinho 2022 Reserva Avesso (Vinho Verde)

A bright fruity wine with a floral aroma and a tangy, vibrant texture, this is full of pink grapefruit and spicy flavors. It comes from an estate established in 1790, a wine that is rich and full in the mouth. Drink from later this year. 91 Points — R.V.

$21 Portugal Vineyards

Anselmo Mendes 2024 Muros Antigos Alvarinho (Vinho Verde Monção e Melgaço)

The wine’s ripe citrus fruits are full and bursting with vitality. The intensity is enhanced by orange zest flavors. The wine has a kiwi and white peach aroma that emphasizes its ripeness. Drink from 2026. 91 Points — R.V.

$17 PJ Wine

title: How Can White Wine Be Made from Red Grapes?
summary:
Winemakers around the world are producing excellent bottlings of White Malbec, White Pinot Noir, and more.

The post How Can White Wine Be Made from Red Grapes? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Have you ever had the elusive and confusing experience of tasting a white wine made from a red grape, such as a White Malbec? I have poured wines like this for friends, and the shocked looks are just priceless. “Wait, isn’t that a red grape? Why is this wine clear?” 

The answer is surprisingly simple. Despite their dark skins, most red grapes contain nearly colorless juice, just the same as white (green) grapes. The color we associate with red wine doesn’t come from the juice—it comes from the skins.

When making a traditional red wine, the juice remains in contact with those skins during fermentation, extracting color, tannin, and structure. But if the grapes are pressed gently and the juice is separated immediately, virtually no color is extracted, if any at all. Without skin contact, the winemaker ends up with a virtually clear white wine made from red grapes.

If you have ever enjoyed a Blanc de Noirs Champagne, you have already experienced this phenomenon. Most Champagne producers have utilized this technique for centuries to create Champagnes by transforming Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier into elegant white sparkling wines. 

Some of Champagne’s most respected houses, including Bollinger, Billecart-Salmon, and Ruinart, have built loyal followings around these distinctive bottlings. Today, winemakers around the world are taking the same approach with still wines, creating some of the wine world’s most intriguing conversation starters.

From White Malbec to White Pinot Noir

Argentina has emerged as the home of White Malbec, with producers such as Trivento and Bodegas Salentein showcasing a brighter and cleaner side of the country’s flagship grape. What’s the winemaking secret, you ask? Chief winemaker of Trivento Winery, Germán Di Cesare, shared his secret: “We pick the grapes extremely early, and add a bit of oxygen to help remove any color coming from the grape.”

These wines boast a combination of green apple and pear aromas, while also displaying red cherries and strawberries, which can be uncommon for still wines. Pair that up with soft tannins and the acidity of a white wine and you have a bottle that is unique and beautifully complex. 

In Oregon, White Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc have both developed something of a cult following. Willamette Valley Vineyards is among the pioneers of White Pinot, with producers including Lange Estate Winery and Left Coast Estate continuing to craft compelling examples. These wines feature the soft red fruit and floral notes you would expect from Pinot, while the lighter pear, citrus, and white peach aromas and flavors give them just the right amount of lift.

White Cabernet Franc (also known as “Blanc Franc”) is also having a moment in Oregon, with producers such as Jackalope Wine Cellars and Leah Jørgensen Cellars leading the way. Leah Jorgensen is credited as the first in America to make still white wine from Cabernet Franc. She aptly points out that, “You wouldn’t make a white wine arbitrarily from just any red grape. Cab Franc has the needed acidity, like Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier in Champagne.” 

These wines tend to have less of the red fruit note, but they still carry that vibrant acidity along with the classic peppery and tobacco notes inherent to the grape.

What to Expect in the Glass

Many of these wines are nearly crystal clear, with only the faintest hints of silver, pale straw, or green reflections. Unlike Chardonnay or Viognier, whose deeper colors can come from lees aging, oak maturation, or controlled oxidation, these wines retain their almost transparent appearance because they experience little oxidation and virtually no skin contact, if any.

What I really love about these “blanc de noirs” still wines is their texture. Since the skins are removed immediately, very few phenolic compounds and virtually no tannins are extracted. The result is a mouthfeel that is softer and smoother than their red counterparts, yet many retain more mid-palate weight than lighter white wines like Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc. Because of the process, they maintain their brightness and vibrancy without the richness and oak influence associated with a full-bodied white.

That versatility makes these wines incredibly food-friendly. They pair beautifully with raw shellfish, grilled fish, roast chicken, charcuterie boards, and dishes that might otherwise leave you debating whether to open a white or a lighter red. These wines spark conversations around the table and keep you and your guests coming back for a second (or maybe even a third!) glass. Oh, and did I mention they are perfect for summer?

I think that’s part of their charm—they can humble even the most experienced wine people. Just when we think we’ve learned all there is to know, a glass of White Malbec or Pinot Noir comes along and reminds us that there are still discoveries waiting around the next corner.

Bottles to Try

Artesano de Argento 2023 White Malbec (Agrelo)

Delicate notes of white flowers perfume the nose. On the palate echoes of those floral notes blend with hints of kiwi, adding a touch of tropical fruit. Light-bodied and refreshing, this white Malbec offers an unconventional expression of the variety with aromatic appeal. Best Buy. 89 Points — Jesica Vargas

$17 Ace Spirits

Open Claim 2023 White Pinot Noir (Mount Pisgah)

Made entirely with estate fruit that aged for 16 months in French oak, none of which was new, this white take on Pinot Noir is dazzling. The wine’s aromas alone are worth the price of admission, as golden raspberries and lemon curd are joined by notes of wet slate and white flowers. Slightly elevated acidity and a bit of tannic structure support flavors like lemon, brioche and toasted filberts. This isn’t a light and wispy-textured wine, as those flavors feel like they are putting down a double coat on the palate. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — Michael Alberty

Concannon Vineyard 2025 Cabernet Franc Blanc Cabernet Franc (Livermore Valley)

This selection is a guilty pleasure. Cabernet Franc has long been a popular planting in the Livermore Valley. But, who would have thought to have minimal skin contact with the juice; which is what creates the Blanc. The aromatics are fresh, lively lychee, papaya, honeydew melon, pineapple, yellow plum, and a dash of allspice on nose. The flavors on the palate are white nectarine, peach, cantaloupe, ripe mango, and clove, with a generous amount of acidity. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

Designed to Shine: The Italian Prosecco That Doubles as a Statement Piece

Whether you’re planning a milestone celebration or simply gathering a small group of friends for an impromptu dinner party, the details can feel overwhelming. There’s a menu to set, a table to shape, a guest list to curate, and, of course, drinks to pour.

Choosing a bottle that looks like it belongs at the table adds to that convivial feeling, which is why Brilla!, premium Italian Prosecco is the preferred choice for so many hosts.

Combining authentic Italian craftsmanship with modern style, Brilla! Prosecco DOC Rosé and Prosecco DOC are an effortless choice to pair alongside classic entertaining fare, from freshly shucked oysters to shrimp cocktail to charcuterie. 

With a delicate and complex bouquet of pear, green apple, and lemon as well as floral notes of acacia and rose, the Rosé is fresh and light on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

Made from Prosecco’s iconic white grape, Glera, known for producing light-bodied, high-acid wines with neutral to fruit-forward aromatics, along with Pinot Noir, the blend offers a round and full-bodied structure. This makes it perfect to enjoy as an aperitif, but also positions it as an ideal accompaniment to Prosciutto e Melone (Cured Ham & Cantaloupe) and grilled fish entrées.

Meanwhile, the crisp and dry profile of the Prosecco DOC feels fresh on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

The pronounced peach and green apple notes set the tone for a decadent evening of al fresco summer dinners and pair impeccably with seasonal favorites likegrilled chicken and peaches. And the iconic sound of popping open a bottle only prolongs guests’ desire to linger at the table for hours, talking long after the meal is complete. 

Don’t be surprised if Brilla!’s distinctive, jewel-inspired bottle design comes up as a topic. The conversation-starting, covetable object reflects the meaning of the Italian word (“to shine”). It’s the ideal choice for hosts who understand that the eyes eat first, and that the style of a tablescape influences how guests feel about the menu, the company, and the celebration to come. 

“Brilla was designed to stand apart long before the first pour,” says a representative from the brand. “Its distinctive patented textured bottle, inspired by the brilliance of cut crystal, transforms every bottle into a statement piece—reflecting the sparkle, elegance, and celebration found inside.”

The Brilla! bottle is the result of a design study that goes beyond a simple wine bottle. Its patented texture is reminiscent of a diamond, and echoes a classic gemstone drop shape.

In the world of diamonds, drop-shaped stones are among the most distinctive and difficult to craft; the symmetry, which is achieved with hard work and dedication during processing, is key to the overall beauty of this stone.

Worn as a ring, earring, or pendant, the shape provides a characteristic elegance with which no other diamond cut can compete; it enhances, romantically and gently, the wearer’s form.

This makes each bottle an effortless gift, requiring no additional gift wrap or presentation.

As a natural bridge between the worlds of fashion, design, and hospitality, Brilla! is a beloved choice for making celebratory, Prosecco-based cocktails, which can signal the start of a brunch or aperitif hour in style.

Some of the most common and popular examples include the Aperol Spritz, Bellini, Mimosa, and Negroni Sbagliato, with Prosecco.

In each of these cocktails, Brilla! adds a layer of sophistication and complexity, and sets the tone for an elevated, elegant occasion that guests will associate with a design-minded host.

title: Was the Wine Industry Worrying About the Wrong Generation?
summary:
New data debunks the myth that Gen Z is drinking less. Baby boomers, on the other hand, are a different story.

The post Was the Wine Industry Worrying About the Wrong Generation? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Gen Z alcohol consumption has climbed to 74%, debunking early fears that younger adults are abstaining entirely.
  • Conversely, Baby Boomers show the steepest drop in alcohol consumption, becoming the true generation of moderation.
  • Younger consumers prioritize social experiences and higher quality drinks over traditional wine cellaring or heavy drinking.

The wine industry can breathe easy. According to a newly-released report from beverage analytics firm IWSR, the alcohol consumption rate amongst Gen Z has risen to 74%, up from 66% three years ago. 

After all the hand-wringing about whether this generation, which includes people born between 1996 and 2010, would ever come around to drinking, the stats are showing that they are. More than 84% of Gen Z (of legal drinking age) have consumed cocktails in the last six months, which is more than any other generation. Gen Z has the second-highest beverage alcohol participation rate (77%) of any generation, slightly behind Millennials. 

“The industry spent a long time asking whether younger consumers were interested in wine, when the more interesting question was why it didn’t seem like they were,” says Tynan Pierce, the wine director at Yes Society, the wine club founded by Antica Terra’s Maggie Harrison. “I don’t think younger drinkers were rejecting wine. I think they were rejecting the way wine was being presented to them.”

Baby boomers, however, are a different story. According to the report, boomers (ages 62 to 80) registered significant declines across all consumption metrics. That demographic—long a stronghold for wine sales—has the lowest consumption rate of any generation. 

While the industry has been fretting about Gen Z sales, a key generation was aging out of wine. Have wine pros been worrying about the wrong generation?

The Kids Are Alright

The good news is that 20-somethings are spending money in the alcohol sector. Sure, wine is splitting sales with ready-to-drink cocktails, coolers, and the like, but they’re not vaping instead or abstaining entirely, as early reports suggested.

“The narrative that Gen Z is the generation of moderation is now conclusively debunked,” says IWSR President and Managing Director Marten Lodewijks.

However, as the IWSR report points out, this young generation is interacting with alcohol differently than their elders did.

For one, Gen Z is a cocktail crowd—84% have consumed cocktails in the last six months. They center alcohol around occasions: 18% reported that their last drink was enjoyed in the context of gatherings with five or more people (so, parties.)

Drew Brady, wine director at Ravi DeRossi’s Long Count (and one of Wine Enthusiast’s 2023 Future 40), has noticed that what Gen Z lacks in drinking culture knowledge, they make up for with a love of events, nights out, and occasions. “It feels like drinking is less of an automatic part of the week—the way it was for us—and more attached to a chosen night out,” Brady says. “

While they may not be collecting as much, or spending in the same way, Gen Z is proving to be particularly appreciative of some of wine’s best qualities—storytelling and connection. 

“They want to know who made the wine, how it was made, and why it works on the menu,” he says. “How does this contribute to their experience? A bottle does not need to be famous, but it does need to feel alive, distinctive, and worth remembering.”

“The biggest shift we’re seeing is from accumulation to curation,” says Tyson. “Previous generations often viewed wine through the lens of building a cellar, while younger consumers tend to view wine as something to be opened, shared, and experienced.”

A recent study funded by Bacardi seconded this, finding that Gen Z tends to drink earlier in the day rather than late at night, at occasions rooted around socializing. The Bacardi report also found that 70% of emotionally engaged consumers will spend twice as much on brands they connect with.

“Gen Z is not necessarily rejecting alcohol,” says Charles Ewudo, founder and CEO of PCN Entertainment, a nightlife giant spanning clubs, cocktail bars, and drinks brands. “They are rejecting outdated ways of discovering and engaging with brands … The alcohol industry has viewed Gen Z’s changing relationship with drinking as a challenge, but I think it’s important to recognize that Gen Z is also showing brands where the future of consumer behavior is headed.”

The IWSR’s Lodewijks confirms this: “While Gen Z consumers are creating new patterns for engaging with beverage alcohol, the evidence demonstrates that Gen Z consumers enjoy drinking at roughly the same levels as the rest of society.”

OK, Boomer

While the kids are alright, the IWSR’s report flagged that boomers are not. Drinking continues to decline among the demographic. Boomers reported the smallest number of drinking occasions of any generational cohort and reported consuming the smallest number of drinks when they do drink (an average of 2.6 drinks per occasion). 

“Boomer drinking has been tailing off for several years,” says Lodewijks. This is unsurprising for consumers hitting their 60s and 70s—people grow older, health goals shift.

“These latest Bevtrac results, however, show bigger-than-expected drops in boomer drinking across all major metrics,” he continues. “If this trend continues, it may actually be the boomers, not Gen Z, who deserve the title ‘generation of moderation.”

Moderation Moment

Adding to the fuddle of this all, a global moderation movement has impacted how all demographic groups interact with alcohol. 

49% of Gen Z drinkers reported they are likely to listen to government health guidelines. While consumption rates are steady across all generations, frequency of occasion and amount consumed on each occasion are down—3.9 drinks per occasion, down from 4.4 drinks in 2025.

Thankfully, this reflects a general shift towards a less-but-better approach to alcohol consumption. Last year’s IWSR BevTrac report noted that Gen Z consumers buy less, but do spend more when they make a purchase.

“Gen Z is not consuming mass quantities at the low end, and instead drinking higher quality wines,” says Tim Willard, partner at wine bar Madeira Park. “This generation seems undaunted by the mystery of wine—their comfort zone is exponentially larger than previous generations.”

He finds his restaurant is a playground for all generations, so he gets a front-row seat to the way people actually engage with wine. 

“I think the most important shift is Gen Z’s attitude on quality with little regard for the appellation system,” he says. “It’s actually having a bottom-up effect on older generations, who seem more open to trying wine from less familiar-to-them grapes and places.”

The Takeaway

Is the fact that boomers are spending less on wine a reason to panic? Not likely. This generational shift reflects a changing of a guard, a signal of where big wine powers should shift focus towards. 

“Boomers have historically been some of the most loyal alcohol consumers, but loyalty does not mean immunity to shifting behaviors,” says Ewudo. “As this generation gets older, health, wellness, lifestyle changes, and moderation are impacting consumption habits.”

In short? “The industry cannot assume that yesterday’s loyal customer will consume the same way tomorrow. “

title: At Some Bars, 23 Is the New 21
summary:
To keep rowdy teenagers and inexperienced palates away, a growing slew of cocktail bars across the world are upping the age requirement to 23.

The post At Some Bars, 23 Is the New 21 appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • In Puerto Rico, some cocktail bars are enforcing restrictions above the legal drinking age of 18 to discourage rowdy behavior.
  • Higher age requirements are gaining traction worldwide at bars in cities like Dublin, Stockholm, and New York.
  • Bar owners use these policies to curate a more mature atmosphere for older patrons who appreciate craft cocktails and tip.

Tucked away in the cobblestoned streets of Old San Juan, Puerto Rico, La Factoría— named the best bar in the Caribbean by North America’s 50 Best Bars—is a complex of seven interconnected spaces, a veritable nightlife multiverse that includes a quiet wine bar, a salsa club with live music, and a candle-lit speakeasy. Though every space has its own appeal, for many people, the bar’s biggest draw is what it doesn’t have: guests under 23 years of age.

Puerto Rico‘s legal drinking age is 18, so weekends in nightlife districts typically see crowds of teenagers and young adults bar hopping or drinking in the street. Some are locals and some are wide-eyed American mainlanders who’ve come to the island to get their first (legal) drink. Increasingly, some high-end Puerto Rican bars are now choosing to close their doors to these youngsters, instead searching for customers who might be more interested in enjoying thoughtfully crafted cocktails than in getting drunk. 

High age restrictions are slowly gaining popularity around the world. Dublin, Ireland, boasts the 23-plus Vintage Cocktail Club, and Stockholm, Sweden, has the 24-plus Soap Bar. On New York’s Upper East Side, The Auction House has barred entrance to anyone under 25 on Fridays and Saturdays since 1993. Earlier this year, Dirty Franks, a Philadelphia dive bar, imposed a 25-and-over rule after a surge in fake IDs, including one for Ben Franklin.

These policies are still far from the norm. But, given La Factoría’s astonishing success despite (or perhaps because of) its restriction, other Puerto Rican bars may follow suit. “We made that decision from the very beginning and maybe it’s spreading,” says Leslie Cofresí, La Factoría’s co-owner. “Maybe it’s all our fault.”

A Bar Scene Grows Up

Fifteen years ago, Puerto Rican cocktail culture was just beginning to come into its own. “It’s a new thing here, having so many cocktail bars,” says Mike Norat, a local World Class-awarded bartender and industry veteran. Instead, most people bought beer at casual open-air spots called chinchorros and drank it in public squares. And rather than specialty cocktails, bars offered simple mixed drinks like rum and coke or vodka with orange juice.

In 2013, La Factoría opened its doors, turning the Puerto Rican bar scene on its head. While there were already great cocktail bars—like the Santurce neighborhood’s legendary Santaella—La Factoría showcased its intentionality right off the bat as the first bar to deny entry to groups of people who could legally drink. “[The age policy] was a way to attract the type of customer that we wanted, and to create a more curated experience,” states Cofresí. And however frustrated this made the youths of Puerto Rico, objections to the policies don’t generally have legal standing, as age isn’t usually a protected class outside of the workplace.  

To Norat, this approach makes total sense. “[Teenagers] didn’t know how to drink, they got too drunk, they looked for trouble, they didn’t spend a lot of money.” Of course, this behavior also deters many older customers, for whom being surrounded by drunk teens is the very definition of hell.

At Aurora, a newly-opened cocktail bar with its own 23-plus age restriction, the thinking is similar. “[Younger people] are starting to drink, starting to go out, exploring and getting to know their palate,” says Ivanna Ortiz, Aurora’s operational manager. “And the cocktail world is so complex and vast that experience has taught us that, at that age, they don’t have the mentality necessary to enjoy a cocktail, or to appreciate the process.” 

Meanwhile, bar staff also benefit from these raised age restrictions. Ortiz claims that it’s common for these young drinkers to complain about unfamiliar tastes and prices, or to mock elaborate garnishes and modern techniques like carbonization or clarification. And because they don’t understand what goes into these higher drink prices, they often don’t leave tips.

Other bars and clubs around the island—including the famous Fifty Eight in Condado’s La Concha Resort—have a minimum age of 21. Some, like Club Brava, switch to 21 on weekends, like many 18+ clubs do in the U.S. to avoid underage drinking. While every 18-year-old in Puerto Rico can legally drink, this helps keep rowdy teenagers away. 

While Aurora initially considered going for the more common 21-plus restriction, Ortiz says the owner ultimately decided on 23 to “play it safe.”

Is the Policy Worth the Trouble?

Of course, not everyone is happy about the restrictions. Cofresí recalls instances in which people have gotten angry or left scathing reviews after being turned away at the door. He still defends the decision: “The people that come in are expecting the restriction. It’s sort of a guarantee of the experience.”

Aurora has had a similar response. “We’ve had negative reactions from people who don’t understand why they can’t come in even if they’re legal adults,” Ortiz acknowledges, but adds, “Our loyal customer base mostly loves that we have those filters because they feel more comfortable.”
